title: Cellar and Visitor
premise: Sable Whitlock, a rationalist property surveyor, is sent to appraise Hollowmere House, where every mirror lags reality by one second — and the lag is growing. He discovers the house's last resident, elderly Iris Vane, has been kept alive by a bargain struck in 1974, when her husband vanished and something in the cellar took his place wearing his face. As the reflections begin showing Sable a life he never lived, he realizes the entity doesn't just imitate people; it replaces them, and it has chosen him as the next resident. To escape, Sable must return what was taken — Iris's husband's remains, hidden beneath the cellar floor — before she signs the sale papers that would bind him permanently to the house. In the end, Sable frees Iris and the trapped husband, but chooses to stay one final night to close the mirrors himself, emerging changed: still a skeptic, but now a skeptic who knows exactly what he saw.
about_author: Dominic Galloway is the pen name of a former building inspector who spent fifteen years cataloguing condemned properties across rural England, collecting the strange things owners whisper about their own houses. He writes horror from a converted chapel with no mirrors in it, which he insists is a coincidence.

chapters.title: The Commission
chapters.summary: Third-person limited from Sable Whitlock. A skeptical surveyor takes a lucrative appraisal job at Hollowmere House, dismissing his firm's unease about its history. The emotional beat is quiet arrogance — Sable believes houses are only wood, plaster, and paperwork, establishing the identity theme of a man defined entirely by what he refuses to see.

chapters.title: One Second Behind
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. During his first walkthrough, he notices a mirror reflecting his movement a beat late. He blames fatigue, then tests it with a stopwatch and gets an impossible result. The beat is creeping doubt — the first hairline crack in a worldview built on measurement.

chapters.title: Mrs. Vane's Terms
chapters.summary: Iris Vane's POV. The frail last resident agrees to sign but insists on odd conditions: no work after dark, and never answer the cellar door. Her chapter reveals fierce love for a husband who 'went away' in 1974, and the dread of a woman guarding a secret for fifty years.

chapters.title: Inventory of Wrong Things
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. Cataloguing the house, he finds rooms whose dimensions don't match the blueprints — extra square footage with no location. He finds a 1974 photograph of Iris and her husband Thomas, and the man in the picture seems to be watching him. Beat: professional curiosity curdling into obsession.

chapters.title: The Cellar Door Answers
chapters.summary: Dual POV. Late at night, knocking comes from the cellar door — from the inside. Sable nearly opens it; Iris stops him, hand shaking. Their first real conversation begins an unlikely found-family bond between two lonely people defending the same door.

chapters.title: What the Mirrors Show
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. The mirror lag grows to three seconds, and the reflections start showing variations: Sable married, Sable gray-haired, Sable smiling in ways he never has. The entity is offering him lives. Beat: seduction — horror as temptation rather than threat.

Iris's POV, a memory chapter. She recounts the night Thomas went down to the cellar to fix a burst pipe and came back up wrong — polite, attentive, and smelling of cold earth. She buried the truth along with what was left of him under the floorboards. Beat: guilt and love entangled beyond untangling.

chapters.title: The Man Who Appraises Back
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. The house begins appraising him: measurements of his life appear in the survey notes in his own handwriting. His firm calls asking why he hasn't filed reports he remembers filing. Beat: identity erosion — the house is learning to be him.

chapters.title: Found Family, Found Footage
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Sable and Iris share tea and trade truths half-admitted; he fixes her boiler, she teaches him her husband's card game. Warmth blooms deliberately against the darkening house. Beat: tenderness as resistance — love against duty made literal.

chapters.title: The Second Sable
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. He meets himself in the upstairs hallway — not a reflection, but solid, warm-handed, wearing his coat. It apologizes for intruding. Beat: terror fused with uncanny politeness; the replacement has begun and it is courteous about it.

chapters.title: Papers on the Table
chapters.summary: Iris's POV. The buyer's solicitor arrives; signing is set for Friday. Iris wavers — selling means leaving the thing below unguarded, but staying means dying in its keeping. Beat: duty versus mercy, the novel's central dilemma sharpened.

chapters.title: Below
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. He breaks his own rule and descends. The cellar is larger than the house. He finds Thomas's remains wrapped in a tarpaulin marked with Iris's handwriting, and understands the bargain: the entity wears the dead until someone living agrees to take their place. Beat: revelation and revulsion.

chapters.title: The Bargain Read Aloud
chapters.summary: Iris's POV. Confronted, Iris confesses everything — how she fed the thing lies to keep it docile, how it promised Thomas back if she found a replacement. She asks Sable, trembling, to be that replacement. Then immediately begs him to refuse. Beat: shame, need, and love at war in one voice.

chapters.title: Refusal
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. He refuses — not heroically, but out of stubbornness, the same trait that kept him blind. The house retaliates: doors relocate, mirrors multiply, and the second Sable moves in downstairs. Beat: defiance with consequences; the walls literally close ranks.

chapters.title: What Was Taken
chapters.summary: Dual POV. They realize returning the remains properly — named, mourned, reburied above ground — might dissolve the bargain. But the second Sable guards the stairs, and it argues beautifully, using Sable's own memories like currency. Beat: the enemy becomes intimate.

chapters.title: Night of the Long Hallways
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. The house stretches; every corridor leads back to the cellar door. Sable walks for hours, pursued by versions of his own life reflected in every surface. Beat: pure psychological siege — identity reduced to what survives when all your evidence is counterfeit.

chapters.title: Iris Signs
chapters.summary: Iris's POV. Cornered by the solicitor and the house both, Iris signs the papers — and the mirrors go perfectly, instantly still. The silence is worse. She realizes she has traded Sable without meaning to. Beat: devastating quiet; duty completed as betrayal.

chapters.title: The Replacement
chapters.summary: Second Sable's POV (brief, unsettling). The double explains, reasonably, why it deserves the life more: it remembers being loved. Sable, weakened and doubting which of them is original, nearly concedes. Beat: the identity theme at knife-point — memory as the only selfhood.

chapters.title: Digging Up Thomas
chapters.summary: Dual POV. Iris, having signed, uses her last hours in the house to help Sable raise the remains while the second Sable screams through the floorboards in Thomas's voice. Beat: desperate, physical climax-building — two old and young hands pulling floorboards together.

chapters.title: Return What Was Taken
chapters.summary: Climax. In the overgrown garden, they bury Thomas properly, speaking his name aloud. The house convulses; the mirrors shatter outward; the second Sable unravels into the shape of the real Thomas, finally released. The entity, unmasked and unbargained, recedes into the sealed cellar. Beat: grief transmuted into release.

chapters.title: The Last Resident
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. Iris leaves for her sister's, alive and free, calling Sable 'the son I didn't bury.' He stays one final night alone to verify the mirrors are dead — a choice, not a compulsion. Beat: resolution of love-against-duty; he stays because he chooses to, not because the house says so.

chapters.title: Appraisal Complete
chapters.summary: Epilogue, Sable's POV. He files his report marking Hollowmere uninhabitable, keeps one shard of mirror glass as a paperweight, and visits Iris monthly. The final line: he still doesn't believe — he knows, which is different, and heavier. Beat: hard-won peace; a skeptic rebuilt around a truth he can never prove.
